item.title: Thought-Watching for Athletes and Others
item.description:
Sport and Competition

Thought-Watching for Athletes and Others

You can benefit from observing your thoughts.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • Anyone can benefit from learning to observe their thoughts without believing them or taking them personally.
  • It's common for people have negative internal chatter and self-­critical play-­by-play.
  • You can learn to notice thoughts and feelings without judging them as good or bad, right or wrong.
  • Athletes (and others) can free themselves from judgments that might unnecessarily determine their limits.

Let’s begin with a challenging drill: What thoughts and feelings appear as you read the words “Let's begin with a challenging drill?” Do you have a sense of “Let’s do this!” or “Ugh, I’m not in the mood”? Are you curious? Excited? Nervous? Simply notice whatever thoughts and feelings show up without judging them as good or bad, right or wrong.

OK, now here’s the challenge. Get four large paper clips and your cell phone or a stopwatch. Separate the paper clips and set them on the table. Before you begin, take 10 slow, deep breaths. Then time yourself and, using only your dominant hand (the hand you write with), link all four paper clips together end to end in a chain. Most elite athletes can do this task in 30 seconds.

Before you begin, though, there is one additional part to the exercise: While you connect your paper clips, do your best to notice your thinking. When you are ready, start your timer and begin. Stop the timer when you have linked all four paper clips.

What did you say to yourself, either internally or out loud? Were your thoughts kind or unkind? Helpful or unhelpful?

Do you have thoughts like these when you are training and competing? Or when you are doing homework, taking a test, working on a project, or talking to someone you are interested in?

If some, or a lot, of your internal dialogue is unkind, unhelpful, and untrue, please know you are not alone. Most people have this negative internal chatter and self-­critical play-­by-play. I fondly call it Unkind Mind.

As author Grace Lichtenstein writes, Unkind Mind is our real opponent: “Your opponent, in the end, is never really the player on the other side of the net, or the swimmer in the next lane, or the team on the other side of the field, or even the bar you must high-­jump. Your opponent is yourself, your negative internal voices.”

Sports psychologist Keith Kaufman has conducted multiple research studies regarding the benefits of mindfulness in sports. His research supports a primary premise of my book A Still Quiet Place for Athletes: that with practice you can learn to watch Unkind Mind without believing it, taking it personally, or letting it prevent you from fully expressing your talent. "Athletes can learn to recognize their mind wandering toward thoughts about limitations during competition (e.g., 'I can’t sustain this pace') but then mindfully label these experiences as just thoughts, let them go and bring attention back to a present moment anchor like their breathing. Through this process, athletes can free themselves from judgments that might unnecessarily determine their limits."

And everyone—athletes, business people, performing artists, health care providers, young people, parents—can benefit from learning to observe their thoughts without believing them or taking them personally.

During the next week, practice simply noticing your thoughts without believing them or taking them personally. See if it helps you in your daily life—in training and competition, at work or school, on stage, or in your relationships.

This post is adapted from my book A Still Quiet Place for Athletes: Mindfulness Skills for Achieving Peak Performance and Finding Flow in Sports and in Life.

item.title: The Tuning Forks of Life
item.description:
Beauty

The Tuning Forks of Life

How groups make beautiful music together.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • Making music together represents an extraordinarily complex form of human coordination.
  • Shared rhythmic movement blurs the boundary between individual identity and collective connection.
  • Individual notes blend into a grand symphony, evidence that human existence is never a solo performance.
  • Effective groups develop habits of attunement, adapting to members’ needs, contributions, and rhythms.
Source: Ashley Brody Photography/Used with permission

Before the orchestra begins, the oboe plays an A, and the musicians listen and tune their instruments. By the time the conductor raises the baton, the hall has been filled with the sound of people getting ready to play together.

When you spend time behind the scenes at a Loudoun Symphony Orchestra concert, you begin to notice how many people help make the evening possible. Executive Director Karen Knobloch attends to one set of details. Board President Andrew Bluhm and the board handle others. Someone raises money, and someone else publicizes the concert. The program has to be written, edited, designed, printed, and delivered before anyone in the audience opens it.

Andrew Bluhm, Board President
Source: Ashley Brody Photography/Used with permission

Onstage, the preparations are just as specific. The crew places chairs, music stands, the podium, and risers for the singers. Someone checks the lights; someone else checks the sound. Stephan and his colleagues take tickets while a volunteer hands out programs. A stage technician spots a chair three inches out of place and moves it.

These tasks—many routine, some tedious—are easy to overlook when they go well, but they're vital: A missed detail can cause trouble just as the evening is about to begin.

Loudoun Symphony Orchestra
Source: Ashley Brody Photography/Used with permission

When Beethoven’s Ninth began at a recent concert, concerns about fundraising goals, rehearsal schedules, and printer deadlines fell away, and everyone's attention shifted to the stage. We followed a phrase from one section to another, felt the force of the crescendo, then leaned in during a quieter passage. When the chorus entered, I found myself thinking about how much had to happen before those voices could fill the hall. And what voices they were.

We may come to hear a familiar work, but the musicians still have to play it together in the moment. They follow their own parts while watching the conductor and listening to players nearby. Entrances must be precise. A phrase needs room to unfold. If the timing shifts, each player has to respond.

From our seats, we don’t hear every adjustment. We hear when a phrase holds together, when an entrance feels sure, when the musicians give a soloist space. Watch closely, and you can see how much attention each player sustains.

Hayden Denesha, Loudoun Symphony Orchestra
Source: Ashley Brody Photography/Used with permission

What helps a group function well?

At work meetings, people learn who needs time to think before speaking, who keeps track of the details, and whether a difficult question will be taken seriously. At home, one family member may need a few quiet minutes after work, while another may want to talk the minute they get in the door. Groups develop these habits—these forms of attunement—over time, often without discussing them.

Sometimes a small gesture can make a difference in how a group interacts. Maybe someone explains a decision instead of assuming everyone is on the same page, or a colleague might check in after a hard meeting.

When these customs or rules aren't respected, or when they fail, group effectiveness suffers. For instance, when people don’t know who can make a decision, meetings drag on. Family members may repeat themselves when they don’t feel heard. Colleagues who are otherwise capable of good work may waste too much time working around one another.

We tend to focus on the visible event: the concert, the meeting, the dinner, or the presentation. We're less likely to notice the conditions that made the event come together. Who ensured that everyone arrived on time and ready? Who provided necessary information to others? Who made sure everyone knew their role? What structures and systems were in place for people to raise concerns?

For an orchestra, small, seemingly inconsequential things can make a big difference. Moving a chair can help a musician see the conductor. The risers need to be checked before the chorus takes its place. An email answered before rehearsal can settle a question that might have caused problems or been a distraction had it been ignored.

Before the downbeat

Karen Knobloch, Executive Director of the Loudoun Symphony Association, Inc.
Source: Ashley Brody Photography/Used with permission

Any leader can ask similar questions to help a group perform well, whether that's an orchestra, family, or a work team. Do people actually hear one another? Are responsibilities clear? Has an awkward arrangement become so familiar that everyone simply works around it?

We can also take time to notice those whose work fades into the background when everything goes smoothly. At a concert, we applaud the musicians and the conductor, but we may never meet the volunteer at the door again, or know who solved a logistical problem that afternoon. Yet our evening still depended on their care and competence.

Each musician brings a different part to the performance. During the Ninth, we watched the players follow the conductor and listen across the stage. When the soprano entered, the sound in the room changed. In rehearsal, musicians learn when to bring their part forward and when to leave room for someone else.

By the time the audience sees the stage, the cables are in place, chairs have been moved, phone calls have been made, and the musicians have rehearsed. We may never know who moved that chair or secured the donation, but by the time the music begins, their work is already part of the evening.

item.title: Cultivating Solitude
item.description:
Self-Help

Cultivating Solitude

Why time alone fosters self-connection and inner balance.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • Many people avoid solitude, fearing it as aloneness.
  • Solitude can bring some people closer to troubling thoughts than they want to be.
  • With thoughtfulness or a therapist's help, we can cultivate and enjoy solitude.

“Solitude,” wrote C.G. Jung, “is for me a fount of healing which makes my life worth living.” For me, too. Now. But it wasn’t always so. For a lot of us, solitude can have a chilling resemblance to aloneness. Memoirist Anne Lamott speaks for others who fear solitude when she says, “My mind is a bad neighborhood I try not to go into alone.”

Until my late 20s, solitude was something I tolerated. Barely. I braced for it. Filled it with soothing treats like chocolate chip cookies or colorful magazines or symphonic music that helped me bear the inexplicable dread I felt there, the terrible isolation. I hadn’t yet developed close friendships that might have made me feel a part of the social flow. And in that panicky state of dread that I never would be a part of it, I didn’t have the patience or faith to try to create social connections. Where my peers just assumed they’d meet their true loves and soul mates, I thought it seemed quite improbable. Although my therapist assured me that connecting was human nature and eventually that would seem true to me, it wasn’t until then that I began to recognize the pleasures of solitude.

There’s a reason for this. The esteemed British pediatrician and psychoanalyst D.W. Winnicott explained that “the basis of the capacity to be alone is a paradox; it is the experience of being alone while someone else is present.” Small children begin to play by themselves and develop the capacity for solitude when they feel secure that a loving caregiver is nearby. In adult life, as in my case, that security comes from feeling a sense of community and social life, good friends, and family closeness.

Discovering Companionship Through Reading

Solitude revealed its charms in my life with reading. I’d always loved novels but hadn’t recognized how the stories and the characters could feel like companions—and how a novel on my night table began to feel as good as a friend at my kitchen table. And sometimes, it felt even better. In the quiet engagement with the world on the page, all my feelings and thoughts about it became vivid. I’d be flooded with appreciation of the great gift of that author’s story and the excitement of inhabiting another person’s mind. Gradually, I filled the bookshelves I constructed from bricks and wood planks.

In my early 30s, finding myself alone for long stretches in a country setting, I began to notice that going on solitary hikes, which I’d never done before, brought me the feeling of well-being and wonder that novels did. Alone in the quiet of a mountain trail, I saw the minute detail of each tree and berry bush, the creek below and the stony hilltop, and even the path itself that someone had cleared and groomed. They were all my companions. It was as if solitude had become a voice that I could now hear, and was finding it had so much to say—about beauty, about nature’s magnitude, and the magnitude within. That is, I was beginning to find a companionship with myself.

It took some years to learn that in solitude, you’re not alone—you’re with yourself. It seems obvious, but was surprising to me. I hadn’t known that being with yourself could be a pleasure, a luxury even, though you may need a therapist, as I did, if your mind seems like a bad neighborhood.

Solitude as a Source of Healing and Balance

Eventually, solitude became a necessity for me, a place to heal, as Jung wrote, and to rebalance whatever’s gone off kilter in the toss of everyday life. I’d begun to feel beckoned by it, as if I were going to meet a friend. Though that friend is myself, it’s often a part of me that’s not always present or active, but waits for the invitation and the right conditions. When I have them, I listen carefully, the way I would to someone I care about. I’m alert to what I discover in my own mind, including the confusing parts, the scary ones, the sadnesses, and those trippy far corners I rarely reach in the company of others.

In my life, the pleasures of solitude are most reliably found on a hike or in meditation. But sometimes it happens in my office when I’m writing, or in my kitchen on a long afternoon making soup and baking lemon squares. It’s no longer just an activity to prepare for another better activity that involves people. It’s the pleasure of solitude in itself.

Though nature and meditation are common places to find solitude, I’ve learned it can be found in the least likely places as well. A yoga teacher once explained to the class that yoga was developed to create a private inward space where people who live in densely populated places can retreat to be alone. And it worked, he said, having himself grown up as one of five children in a crowded three-generation New Delhi household. I have a friend who only goes to movies alone to truly appreciate this art form she loves, and for her, that’s solitude. Another friend, a gracious host with ample room for her visitors’ long stays, lets guests know not to talk to her before mid-morning though she might be sitting at the table reading the paper. It’s how she manages to start the day with the solitude she needs.

Everyone, it seems, has to find their own solitude, then cultivate it and maintain it, just as you would a friendship. So, what does solitude offer? An underlying harmony, an equilibrium despite whatever difficulty or disappointment you find yourself in. Its real gift, though, is that it gives you yourself, and maybe healing, like Jung says, and sometimes, it gives you what feels like everything.

item.title: Turn Conflicts Into Opportunities
item.description:
Relationships

Turn Conflicts Into Opportunities

Conflicts are inevitable and yet offer significant opportunities for growth.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • Conflicts offer an opportunity to understand other perspectives.
  • Conflicts can help us clarify our limitations, values, and needs.
  • Viewing conflicts as opportunities can soften our negative response to them.
Source: Jean Wimmerlin / Unsplash

During a psychotherapy session, a single mother, whom I’ll call Deb, lamented that her 3-year-old daughter had been screaming and throwing fits every time she had to wash her hands. Deb found the lead-up to dinner each day a horrific power struggle when her daughter kicked, screamed, and cried when her mother led her to the sink to wash her hands.

“This nightly power struggle is going to break me,” Deb said. “I have no idea why she suddenly finds handwashing so awful.”

“Did you ask her what upsets her so much about handwashing?” I asked.

“No, I just tried telling her how it kills germs, it’s important to keep her from getting sick, it’s good manners; nothing seems to work,” Deb said.

I suggested to Deb that this conflict with her child was an opportunity to better understand her daughter’s distress. “Maybe try a different approach and see if it works. Maybe this evening, don’t take her to wash her hands. Instead, sit with her and talk a bit. Then tell her you’d like to know what upsets her about handwashing. Make it your goal to understand why she’s upset, rather than force her to wash her hands,” I said.

Deb felt desperate and agreed to try that approach. At our next session, she smiled and said, “You won’t believe what happened! I did what you said, and my daughter said, ‘It hurts.' I asked her, ‘What hurts?’ and she said, ‘My eye hurts.’ Apparently, she once got soap in her eye, and it hurt, so she thought it would happen every time she washed her hands. So, I said, ‘Mommy can help you do it, so it won’t hurt,’ and you know what? She washed her hands with me, no problem. I showed her how to be careful and keep the soap out of her eyes. Unbelievable. I had no idea.”

While this may seem like a simple example, most conflicts offer an opportunity to better understand another person’s experience. After decades of providing couples counseling, I can report that relationships improve when people put more energy into understanding one another rather than focusing on their own agenda.

Conflicts Deepen Understanding

Conflicts offer a window into another person's unique individuality. When you can take another person’s perspective and understand it, as Deb eventually did with her daughter, the conflict becomes a catalyst for positive change.

Research shows we are happier in relationships where the other person can understand our point of view. That requires spending quality time with others where we can enjoy relaxed conversations (Jiao, et al. 2026). When Deb stopped trying to make her daughter obey and instead sat down with her to listen, she created the quality time needed to understand her daughter’s concern.

Opportunities for Growth

Phyllis Olins is a conflict mediator and the author of the new book, The Conflict Crunch: How to Turn Conflict into Opportunity. She writes, “Your conflict may nudge you out of a personal rut.” It is easy to fall into rigid thinking and behavior, like the daily argument Deb and her daughter engaged in. Relationships can stagnate when we aren’t willing to look at ourselves and change.

Sometimes relationship conflicts, such as a serious marital crisis, can break our hearts and shake us to the core. Olins writes that “the scariest chapters of your life are the moments where growth can occur.” We learn more about our limitations, our deepest values, and what we’re willing and unwilling to do for our relationships. We also have an opportunity to learn more about our partner’s limitations, values, and needs.

Many couples enter counseling after a significant crisis, such as an affair or the revelation of a long-kept secret. They work together to understand the cause of the crisis and their underlying fears, needs, and values. Over time, many report a stronger, deeper connection and commitment to one another. The crisis forces them to face one another, peeling away layers of secrecy and fear, and reaching a deeper level of trust and acceptance.

Conflict at Work

Conflicts at work are inevitable. As companies globalize their workforce, opportunities for disagreements, misunderstandings, miscommunications, and frustrations multiply. Leaders need strong conflict-management skills and processes to prevent negative outcomes such as high employee turnover, absenteeism, and sabotage. When companies implement clear, structured conflict management processes and procedures, employee morale improves. When managers adopt collaborative, cooperative conflict-management practices, they can enhance the performance of the entire organization (Sanjeevan et al., 2025).

Constructive conflict management includes:

  1. Identifying the real problem.
  2. Taking on the issue early and visibly.
  3. Communicating clearly and calmly.
  4. Viewing conflict as a negotiation.
  5. Lowering the emotional temperature.
  6. Showing respect (Lewis et al. 2025).

When we look at conflicts as opportunities, we might relax our negative responses just enough to make room for greater understanding. With greater understanding, we will likely make better decisions and grow.
